passage: Quarterly disclosure of Halloway Fastener Works, filed with the Bureau of Industrial Registration, period ending September 30. The company reports revenue of 4.2 million dollars for the quarter, against 3.9 million dollars in the same quarter last year, an increase attributable chiefly to the marine hardware line introduced in February. Operating expenses rose to 3.5 million dollars, driven by a 9 percent increase in zinc costs and by overtime associated with the recall described in item 7. Item 7: on August 4 the company initiated a voluntary recall of lot 2214 of its half inch galvanized turnbuckles after internal testing found tensile strength below the declared rating in samples drawn from a single heat of wire. Approximately 18,000 units shipped; 11,400 have been returned to date. No failures in service have been reported. The recall reserve is set at 260,000 dollars. The company further discloses the retirement of director Elspeth Mangold, effective October 15, and the appointment of Uri Castellanos to the audit committee. Headcount at quarter end stood at 212, up from 199. No material litigation is pending. The next scheduled filing is due January 30.
question: Which lot of turnbuckles was subject to the voluntary recall?

passage: Application for a discharge permit, submitted by Renwick Dye and Finishing to the Water Quality Board, docket W-4471. The applicant seeks authorization to discharge treated process water to the Sotter River at a maximum rate of 120,000 gallons per day, an increase from the 85,000 gallons per day authorized under the expiring permit. The increase reflects the planned addition of a second finishing line in the spring. The applicant proposes to meet the increase without raising the thermal load by installing a plate heat exchanger that returns recovered heat to the dye vats; modeling attached as Exhibit C predicts effluent temperature at the outfall will in fact decline by 2 degrees. Treatment remains as currently configured: screening, equalization, biological treatment, and sand filtration, with sludge hauled to the Copeland facility under contract 88-C. The applicant notes one exceedance in the past five years, a color violation in March of the second year, traced to a torn filter membrane and corrected within 36 hours. Monitoring is proposed weekly for color and metals and continuously for flow and temperature. A public comment period of 45 days is requested to begin upon publication.
question: What maximum daily discharge rate does the applicant seek?

passage: Notice of proposed rulemaking, Office of Weights and Measures, reference WM-2031. The Office proposes to amend rule 14.3 governing the verification of fuel dispensers to require testing of each retail dispenser once every 12 months, replacing the current 24 month cycle. The proposal follows a three year audit in which 6.1 percent of dispensers tested at the 24 month mark were found outside tolerance, compared with 2.3 percent at 12 months, with the average error at failing dispensers amounting to an overcharge of 31 cents per fill. The Office estimates the change will require four additional field inspectors and raise annual program costs by 410,000 dollars, to be recovered through an increase in the per dispenser registration fee from 30 dollars to 46 dollars. Small operators with three or fewer dispensers may elect a certified third party inspection in place of the state visit, a provision carried over unchanged from the existing rule. Comments will be received for 60 days from publication and a hearing will be held on the first Thursday of the third month at the Office's Landis Street hearing room. Absent substantive objection, the rule takes effect on the following July 1.
question: What percentage of dispensers tested at the 24 month mark were outside tolerance?

passage: Annual safety summary of the Verlaine Aerial Tramway, submitted to the Passenger Ropeway Authority as required by section 9 of the operating license. The tramway carried 384,000 passengers in the reporting year across 21,600 completed trips, with an availability of 96.2 percent against the licensed minimum of 92 percent. Lost service divided as follows: 41 hours for scheduled maintenance, 63 hours for wind holds, and 19 hours for unscheduled stoppages, the longest of which, seven hours on November 9, resulted from a faulty brake sensor on the counterweight carriage and is the subject of corrective action CA-118, closed January 12 with replacement of all four sensors of the affected type. Two passenger injuries were recorded, both minor: a wrist sprain during boarding attributed to a wet platform, after which grooved matting was installed at both stations, and a finger laceration from a door hinge, after which hinge guards were fitted to all eight cabins. The haul rope, installed six years ago, was examined magnetically in May; wire breaks were found within norms, and the next rope examination falls due in 24 months. The operator certifies the evacuation drill was completed October 3 with 61 participants.
question: What caused the seven hour unscheduled stoppage on November 9?

passage: Application for zoning variance, parcel 114-062, filed by Mirena Holt, doing business as the Salt Meadow Creamery. The applicant operates a licensed dairy processing kitchen in an agricultural zone and seeks a variance to permit retail sales on the premises for up to 30 hours per week, where the zone by right allows farm stands selling only unprocessed goods. The property fronts Quarry Road for 410 feet and contains the residence, the creamery building of 2,200 square feet, and a gravel lot of eleven spaces installed last year under permit 09-441. The applicant states that 70 percent of production, chiefly soft cheeses and bottled milk, is now sold at markets in three towns, requiring 240 road miles weekly, and that on site sales would cut vehicle trips rather than add them, an assertion supported by a traffic memorandum from Corliss Engineering estimating a net reduction of 14 trips per week. Two neighbors have filed letters: one in support, one objecting to weekend noise. The applicant offers conditions: no sales before 9 a.m. or after 6 p.m., no amplified sound, and signage limited to one board of six square feet. The board of appeals hears the matter on April 11.
question: How many parking spaces does the gravel lot contain?

passage: Incident report filed with the Pipeline Safety Division by Norgard Transmission Company, report number PR-887. On June 2 at 03:14, pressure monitoring at the Elk Bend compressor station recorded a drop of 8 percent over eleven minutes on line 4, triggering automatic closure of block valves 41 and 43 and isolation of a 6.2 mile segment. A field crew dispatched at 03:40 located the cause at 07:55: a leaking gasket on a metering skid flange within the station fence, not a line break. Estimated release: 1.1 million cubic feet of natural gas, all vented to atmosphere; no ignition occurred and no evacuation was ordered, though as a precaution the county was notified at 04:02 under the mutual notification agreement. The gasket, a spiral wound type installed during the 2019 skid rebuild, failed at a location where bolt tension measurements taken after the event were found 30 percent below specification on three of eight studs. Corrective actions: replacement of the gasket and studs, completed June 3; torque verification on all 14 flanges at the station, completed June 11, which found two further flanges below specification; and a fleet wide review of torque records due September 30. Line 4 returned to service June 4.
question: What was found to be the cause of the pressure drop on line 4?

passage: Prospectus summary, Fenholm Water Cooperative, offering of capital notes. The cooperative, which supplies drinking water to 3,400 connections in the Fenholm valley, offers notes in the aggregate amount of 2 million dollars, in denominations of 500 dollars, bearing interest at 4.5 percent, maturing in ten years. Proceeds fund two projects: replacement of the Ridge Road storage tank, a 1958 steel tank of 400,000 gallons to be replaced with a 600,000 gallon concrete tank, budgeted at 1.4 million dollars; and extension of mains to the Garnet Hollow settlement, 62 households now on private wells, budgeted at 450,000 dollars, with the remainder funding issuance costs and a contingency. The cooperative reports operating revenue of 1.9 million dollars and a debt service coverage ratio of 1.8 in the latest audited year. Risks disclosed include: the cooperative's single source, the Fenholm springs, which in the drought of 2018 fell to 61 percent of normal flow for nine weeks; pending renewal of the withdrawal license in year three of the note term; and construction cost escalation. Notes are unsecured, are not insured deposits, and are offered only to persons resident in the service area. The subscription period closes November 30.
question: What interest rate do the offered notes bear?

passage: Petition to the Transport Rates Commission, docket TR-559, filed by Marbeck Ferries. The petitioner seeks approval to raise the vehicle fare on the Cully Sound crossing from 18 dollars to 22 dollars and the foot passenger fare from 5 dollars to 6 dollars, the first increase sought since the current tariff took effect seven years ago. In support, the petitioner submits audited statements showing fuel expense up 64 percent over the tariff period, insurance up 41 percent, and wage costs up 28 percent under the crewing agreement ratified last spring, against ridership essentially flat at 610,000 passengers and 240,000 vehicles annually. The petitioner further states that the vessel Iron Duchess requires her twenty year survey within 30 months at an estimated 900,000 dollars, toward which the company holds reserves of 350,000 dollars. Without relief, the petition states, the company would defer the survey to the statutory limit and reduce winter service from six daily round trips to four. The commission's staff analysis, appended, verifies the cost figures but recommends a vehicle fare of 21 dollars, finding the petitioner's projected maintenance escalator overstated. Interventions must be filed within 21 days; the commission will sit at the Cully Sound ferry hall.
question: What vehicle fare does the commission's staff analysis recommend?

passage: Environmental compliance report, Tarnow Rendering Company, submitted under consent order CO-2288, reporting month of March. Odor complaints received by the county hotline and forwarded to the company: eleven, of which nine were logged on the two days when the primary scrubber was offline for packing replacement, March 14 and 15. This compares with 31 complaints in March of last year, before the scrubber upgrade. The replacement packing was installed eight days ahead of the schedule set in the consent order, and stack testing on March 22 measured removal efficiency at 96 percent against the order's requirement of 90 percent. The backup scrubber, whose absence during past outages the order cites as a root cause, remains on schedule for commissioning by August 31; the vessel arrived on site March 9 and sits on its pad awaiting ductwork. One deviation is reported: the continuous monitor on the stack recorded no data for six hours on March 27 following a power interruption, and the company has installed an uninterruptible supply for the monitor, completed April 2, to prevent recurrence. Wastewater parameters remained within limits all month. The next quarterly meeting with the county falls on May 6.
question: What removal efficiency did the March 22 stack testing measure?
